Dart is single-threaded, but Isolates provide TRUE parallelism. Each isolate has its own memory heap and event loop — no shared state, no race conditions. Communication is via message passing (`SendPort`/`ReceivePort`).

Use isolates for heavy CPU work that would block the UI thread:
- Parsing large JSON (>1MB)
- Image processing / resizing
- Cryptography / hashing
- Complex algorithms

### APIs (simplest to most powerful)
- `Isolate.run()` (Dart 2.19+) — one-shot, simplest
- `compute()` (Flutter) — wraps `Isolate.run`, for functions
- `Isolate.spawn()` — full control, for long-lived isolates

Generics let a class or function declare placeholder types that the caller fills in. Dart generics are reified — at runtime you can still ask `value is List<int>` and the answer is correct (unlike Java's erasure).

### Key points
- **Type parameters**: `class Box<T> { T value; }` — `T` is filled in by the caller
- **Bounds**: `class SortedBox<T extends Comparable<T>>` — restricts T to types that implement Comparable
- **Generic methods**: `T first<T>(List<T> xs) => xs[0];` — type is inferred from the argument
- Use `extends` for upper bounds. Dart has no lower bounds.
- **Variance**: Dart collections are covariant by default — `List<int>` is assignable to `List<num>`. This is unsound but ergonomic; the analyzer catches the worst cases.

Extensions bolt methods, getters, setters and operators onto a type you don't own, resolved statically at compile time.

That makes them free at runtime — no wrapper object, no dynamic dispatch, just a direct call to a static function.

### Good uses
- **Domain helpers on primitives** — `String.toSlug()`, `DateTime.isToday`
- Adapter sugar around a third-party API you cannot change
- Replacing a pile of loose top-level utility functions with discoverable methods

### Limits
- **Cannot add fields** — only methods and computed getters/setters
- Cannot override an existing member; the real method always wins
- Resolved by the STATIC type, so `(x as Object).ext()` does not see the extension
- Two extensions declaring the same member on one type are ambiguous — name them and use `import ... show` to pick a winner

### Extension methods vs extension types
- `extension StringX on String` adds behaviour to every String in scope; it is still a String
- `extension type UserId(String value)` declares a distinct zero-cost wrapper type, so the compiler rejects a raw String where a UserId is expected
- Reach for an extension type when you want a NEW type, an extension when you only want new methods

A mixin is a reusable bundle of methods you fold into a class without single-inheritance constraints. A class can mix in many mixins; it can extend only one class.

### Mechanics
- `mixin Logger { void log(String s) => print(s); }` — declared as a mixin, can never be instantiated
- `class Service with Logger {}` — Service gets log() as if it were defined on it
- `mixin Counter on ChangeNotifier` — `on` requires the host class to extend ChangeNotifier so the mixin can call notifyListeners()
- **Method resolution is linearized**: in `class C extends B with M1, M2`, M2's method overrides M1's, which overrides B's
- Since Dart 3 only a `mixin` or a `mixin class` declaration can appear after `with` — an ordinary class can no longer be mixed in

### Mixin vs interface vs inheritance
- **Inheritance** — "is-a" relationship, single parent, shares state
- Interface (`implements`) — contract only, no implementation reuse
- Mixin (`with`) — reuses implementation across an unrelated tree, multiple at a time, no "is-a" claim

Generators produce sequences lazily. Dart has two flavors:

### sync\* — returns Iterable\<T>
- Yields values synchronously, on demand
- Use for in-memory pull-based sequences (paginate, traverse a tree, build combinations)
- `yield` adds one value, `yield*` delegates to another iterable

### async\* — returns Stream\<T>
- Yields values asynchronously over time
- Use for streams you build by awaiting other futures (websocket fan-out, paginated API loop, file reading)
- **Cancellation**: when the stream subscription is cancelled, the function is paused at its current yield. Important to release resources in `try { ... } finally { ... }`.

### When NOT to use
- If you have everything in memory already — return a List or a plain Stream.fromIterable instead
- If your stream is single-event — return a Future, not an async\*

An enhanced enum can declare fields, a const constructor, getters, methods, and implement interfaces.

Available since Dart 2.17, it keeps everything a plain enum guarantees — constant identity, a `values` list, exhaustive switches — while letting each case carry data and behaviour.

### What you get
- Const constructors with named or positional arguments — metadata sits next to the value
- **Methods and getters** — behaviour on the enum instead of a switch helper somewhere else
- `implements` — an enum can satisfy an interface (it still cannot extend a class)
- `values`, `name` and `byName` for free

### Prefer an enum over a sealed class when
- The set of cases is fixed, finite and uniform in shape
- You want constant identity and exhaustive switches
- No case needs per-instance variable data — that requirement is what pushes you to a sealed class

Records are anonymous, immutable, structurally-typed tuples, and patterns destructure values in place.

### Records
- `(int, String)` is positional; `({int id, String name})` is named
- **Built with parentheses**: `final r = (1, 'a');`
- Positional fields are read as `.$1`, `.$2`; named fields by their name
- **Equality is structural** — two records with equal fields are ==
- They replace ad-hoc `Map<String, dynamic>` returns and hand-written `Pair<A, B>` classes

### Patterns
- `if (response case (200, var body)) { ... }` — type test and bind in one step
- `switch (shape) { case Circle(:final r) => ...; case Square(:final side) => ... }`
- Refutable in `switch` and `if-case`, irrefutable in a variable declaration
- A `when` clause adds a guard: `case Circle(:final r) when r > 10 => ...`
- Over a sealed hierarchy the compiler enforces exhaustiveness

Between them they fix the two things Dart used to be clumsy at: returning more than one value, and branching on the shape of data.

A `sealed class` is one whose complete set of subtypes the compiler knows, because every subtype must live in the same library. That closure unlocks exhaustiveness checking in switch expressions: omit a case and you get a compile error, not a runtime surprise.

### Why it matters for state modeling
- Replaces the classic `if (x is Loading) ... else if (x is Loaded) ...` chains that silently break when you add a new case
- **Fits perfectly with patterns** — destructure each subtype in its own arm
- Together with records you get a discriminated-union style without a third-party library

### Rules
- `sealed` types cannot be instantiated directly — only their concrete subtypes
- Subtypes must live in the SAME library file as the sealed parent (or in part-of files)
- Mixing `sealed` with `final`/`base` controls how external libraries can implement or extend your hierarchy

dart:ffi lets Dart call C-ABI functions directly — no MethodChannel, no platform-thread hop, no message serialization. It is the same mechanism behind sqlite3, crypto and most performance-sensitive plugins.

### FFI vs MethodChannel
- **Latency** — FFI is a direct C call (sub-microsecond). MethodChannel hops to the platform thread and serializes the message (~ms).
- **Threading** — FFI can run on any isolate / any thread. MethodChannel is async and platform-thread-bound.
- **API surface** — FFI talks to C symbols. MethodChannel talks to Java/Kotlin/Swift/ObjC. If you need Android Activity APIs, MethodChannel still wins.
- **Memory** — FFI exposes raw pointers. You allocate, you free. There is no GC across the boundary.

### When to use FFI
- Wrapping a C/C++ library you ship as a binary (image codecs, ML, crypto, hashing)
- Hot-loop work on big buffers — avoid the per-message overhead
- Reusing existing native code with a stable C ABI

### Tooling
- `package:ffigen` generates the Dart bindings from the C headers — hand-writing typedefs for a large API is a mistake
- `@Native` external functions plus native assets let a package ship and link its own native code without a manual DynamicLibrary.open

### When NOT to
- Calling platform-specific Kotlin/Swift APIs — those are not C; use MethodChannel or Pigeon
- **One-off, infrequent calls** — channels are simpler and safer

map, where, expand, take and skip all return a lazy view, so the callback does not run until something actually iterates the result.

That laziness is usually a win: `items.where(match).take(3)` stops after the third match instead of filtering the whole list, and a `sync*` generator can describe an infinite sequence because nobody ever asks for all of it.

### Where it bites
- A callback with a side effect never runs. `items.map(save)` looks like a loop and does nothing — use a for loop or forEach.
- The view is recomputed on every iteration. Calling `.length`, then `.first`, then passing it to a widget runs your predicate three times, and if it hits the network or does real work you have tripled the cost.
- The view reads the source live, so mutating the list between creating the iterable and iterating it either shows the new elements or throws a ConcurrentModificationError
- `length` on a lazy `where` walks the entire sequence, which is not what an O(1) length looks like

### The rules that follow
- Call `toList()` (or `toSet()`) as soon as you will use the result more than once, and use `growable: false` when the size is fixed
- Return a List from your own APIs unless laziness is the point; an Iterable in a public signature quietly asks the caller not to iterate twice
- In Flutter, do not build an expensive chain inside build — it re-runs on every rebuild, laziness or not

Type promotion only applies where the compiler can prove the value cannot change between the check and the use.

A local variable or a parameter satisfies that, so after `if (x != null)` the rest of the block sees a non-nullable x. A mutable field does not: another method, another isolate turn or a callback could assign to it in between, so the compiler refuses and you get the familiar "the property can't be unconditionally accessed because the receiver can be null" error.

### What never promotes
- A non-final field, wherever it lives
- A getter, since each call may return something different
- A public final field, because a subclass in another library could override it with a getter
- A local captured and reassigned inside a closure
- A `late` variable

What does promote: locals, parameters, and — since field promotion landed in Dart 3.2 — a final private field accessed from within its own library, including through another object of that type.

The workarounds, in the order I would reach for them:
- Copy the field into a local and check that: two lines, always correct
- **Use a pattern** — `if (user.name case final name?)` binds and narrows in one step, and the same works in a switch
- Make the field `final` and private, which is usually better design anyway
- `!` only where you can genuinely prove it, remembering that it throws at runtime when you are wrong

The same reasoning powers `is` promotion, and an early `if (value is! String) return;` narrows the whole rest of the method.

late lets a non-nullable variable be initialised after its declaration, moving the null check from compile time to run time.

### It does two distinct jobs
- **Deferred initialisation** — `late String _draft;` compiles even though nothing is assigned yet, and reading it before assignment throws a LateInitializationError. This is how a State field gets its value in initState while staying non-nullable.
- **Lazy initialisation** — `late final _controller = build();` runs the initialiser on the FIRST READ, not at construction. That is what lets an initialiser reference `this`, and it means an expensive object costs nothing if nobody touches it.

`late final` without an initialiser is assign-once at run time, which is the honest way to express "set exactly once, later".

### When it is the wrong tool
- The value can legitimately be missing — then it is nullable, and `T?` describes reality while `late` hides a crash
- It is assigned from an async callback. The gap between the first build and the response is real, so model loading and error states instead.
- You are using it to dodge constructor design. If the object needs a dependency, take it as a parameter.

Small print: every read of a late variable carries a run-time check, static and top-level variables are already lazy without the keyword, and a late variable is never type-promoted.

`firstWhere` has no null to fall back on, so when nothing matches it throws a StateError.

The element type is usually non-nullable, so the method cannot invent a return value and throwing is the only honest option. The call works all through development because the item is always there, and fails the first time a filter comes back empty on a real account.

### The dart:core members that fail the same way
- `first`, `last` and `single` on an empty iterable
- `firstWhere` and `lastWhere` when nothing matches
- `singleWhere` on both sides — "No element" for zero matches, "Too many elements" for two
- `reduce` on an empty iterable; `fold` survives it because it takes a seed
- `indexWhere` breaks the pattern and returns `-1`, a sentinel instead of an exception

### What to write instead
- `orElse: () => fallback` when a default genuinely exists. It must return an element of the same type, so it cannot return null unless the element type is already nullable.
- `firstWhereOrNull` from package:collection. dart:core still ships no `firstOrNull` or `firstWhereOrNull`, which is why nearly every Flutter app depends on that package.
- Handle the null once at the call site, ideally with a pattern: `if (items.firstWhereOrNull(test) case final hit?)` binds and narrows in one step.

Rule of thumb: every `...Where` in production code either carries an `orElse` or comes from package:collection. A bare `firstWhere` is a crash waiting for the empty case.

`hashCode`. A hash set picks the bucket by `hashCode` first, so two objects with different hashes never get compared with `==` at all.

The default `hashCode` is an identity hash, unique per instance, so an `==` override on its own is dead code inside any Set or Map.

### The contract
- Equal objects must have equal hash codes. The reverse is not required — collisions are legal and just cost a comparison.
- Build the hash from exactly the fields `==` compares: `Object.hash(a, b)`, `Object.hashAll(list)`, `Object.hashAllUnordered(set)`. Never add or xor field hashes by hand; `a + b` collides for every reordering.
- The signature is `bool operator ==(Object other)` — taking anything narrower than `Object` silently stops overriding the real operator.

### The second trap: mutation
A hash code must not change while the object is a Set element or a Map key. Mutate a field that feeds it and the entry stays in its old bucket: `contains` returns false, `remove` does nothing, and the entry leaks for the life of the map. Keep every field used by `==` final.

### What to use instead of writing it by hand
- Records already have structural equality, so `(userId, day)` is a valid composite Map key with no boilerplate
- freezed, dart_mappable or equatable generate both members from one field list
- Getting it right is what lets `ValueNotifier` skip a notification and `select`-style listeners skip a rebuild when the new value equals the old

Mental model: `==` decides what "the same" means, `hashCode` decides where the runtime looks for it. Ship them together or neither works.

Dart generics are reified, so the decoded value really is a `List<dynamic>` at run time, and `List<dynamic>` is not a subtype of `List<Map<String, dynamic>>`.

`jsonDecode` returns `dynamic`; arrays come back as `List<dynamic>` and objects as `Map<String, dynamic>`. The elements have the shape you expect — it is the outer list's type argument that is wrong, and because Dart keeps type arguments at run time (unlike Java, which erases them) the cast checks that argument and fails with "type 'List<dynamic>' is not a subtype of type 'List<Map<String, dynamic>>' in type cast".

### Three ways out, and the one to pick
- `.cast<T>()` returns a lazy checked view: no copy, but a bad element throws wherever it is finally read, which is usually a widget far from the decode
- `List<T>.from(json)` copies eagerly and throws right here, at the cost of a second list
- `map((e) => Model.fromJson(e as Map<String, dynamic>)).toList()` is the one to reach for. The cast is per element, next to the parse, so the failure names the item and you leave the boundary holding your own model type.
- `whereType<T>()` when a mixed array should be filtered rather than rejected

The trap with `cast` is that it type-checks anywhere, so `List<String> names = raw.cast()` compiles happily and relocates the crash into the UI.

The same reification explains the rest of the family: `<dynamic>[1, 2] is List<int>` is false, while `<int>[1, 2] is List<num>` is true because Dart's generics are covariant. Cast once, at the boundary, into a type you own.

Extension members are resolved at compile time from the static type of the receiver — there is no dynamic dispatch and no entry in the object's interface.

The compiler looks at the declared type of the expression, finds the applicable extensions in scope, and inlines a static call. Nothing about the actual object at run time takes part.

### What follows from that
- `Animal a = Dog(); a.speak()` runs the extension on `Animal`, even though the object is a Dog. An extension is not an override.
- A `dynamic` receiver has no static type to match, so no extension applies and you get a NoSuchMethodError at run time.
- If the type already declares a member with that name, the instance member always wins and your extension is unreachable.
- The extension must be imported at the call site. It is not part of the interface, so a library that does not import it cannot see the member at all.
- Two applicable extensions are a compile error unless one on-type is a strict subtype of the other. Resolve it with explicit application, `Trimmed(s).clean()`, or `show`/`hide` on the import.
- You can extend a nullable type (`extension on String?`) and legally call it on null — something no real method can do.

Rule of thumb: an extension is nicer syntax for a static helper function, scoped by import, not a new virtual method. If the behaviour must vary by the object's real type, you want an interface or a sealed hierarchy; if it just needs to read the object, an extension is exactly right.

Every evaluation of a closure expression creates a new function object, so you are asking the notifier to remove a function it has never been given.

`removeListener` searches its list by equality. The closure you passed to `addListener` and the closure you wrote in `dispose` are two different objects that happen to have the same body, and Dart does not consider them equal. The listener stays, fires after dispose, and you get "setState() called after dispose()" — or a leak, since the notifier now holds your State alive.

### What Dart actually guarantees about function identity
- A tear-off of the same instance method on the same object is `==` — `c.onChange == c.onChange` is true, though `identical` is false, since Dart 2.15 made tear-off equality well defined
- Tear-offs of static and top-level functions are canonical and always equal
- Different receivers give unequal tear-offs: `Counter().onChange != Counter().onChange`
- Two closure expressions are never guaranteed equal, capturing or not, so a closure cannot be used as a removal key

### The rule that follows
Anything you will have to remove, cancel or compare later gets a name: a method tear-off (`_refresh`) or a field holding the closure once. The same applies to `removeObserver`, `removeStatusListener` and any hand-rolled `Set<VoidCallback>` registry.

The other cost is rebuild diffing: a fresh closure per build makes the widget unequal every frame, so it can never be `const` and any `==`-based short circuit always says "changed".

The mixins are applied left to right on top of the superclass, so the chain is Base → Logging → Caching → Repo, and `super` inside Logging means Base.

Each `with` clause builds an anonymous synthetic class: `Base with Logging` is one class, that class `with Caching` is the next, and Repo extends the last one. So the rightmost mixin sits closest to your class and wins any name conflict, while `super` inside a mixin points one link to its left.

### Reading the chain
- `Repo().describe()` runs Repo's body first; each `super.describe()` steps left, ending at Base. The verified output is `Repo(Caching(Logging(Base)))`.
- Ask "who wins a conflicting member?" and read right to left. Ask "what does `super` see?" and read left to right.
- Two mixins declaring the same member is not an error and produces no warning — the rightmost silently replaces the other.

### The constraints that catch people
- `on Base` is the superclass constraint. It restricts where the mixin can be applied and is what makes `super.describe()` type-check; without it `super` is Object and the mixin can only add members, never wrap them.
- A mixin cannot declare a constructor, so it cannot take parameters. Expose an abstract getter and let the class supply the value.
- Since Dart 3 a plain class can no longer be used as a mixin: declare `mixin class`, which in turn must not declare a constructor.
- In Flutter this is why an `initState` override inside a mixin must call `super.initState()` — skip it and every mixin to its left stops running.

Measure the size of what crosses the boundary: both directions of the hop deep-copy the message, and that copy runs on the sending isolate, so a big payload costs you the very frame you were trying to save.

`compute` is a thin wrapper over `Isolate.run` (Dart 2.19+): spawn an isolate, run the closure, terminate it. Spawning is cheap because isolates in a group share a heap, but `SendPort.send` copies the transitive object graph in linear time. Only values the runtime knows are immutable — numbers, bool, null, strings — are shared instead of copied.

### Where the time actually goes
- Decoding on the UI isolate and then sending the resulting `Map` tree pays for the decode *and* a copy of every node
- Returning a large `List<Model>` copies it back, again on the worker's side of the wire
- A closure passed to `Isolate.run` captures its surrounding scope, so capturing `this` inside a State can drag the widget tree along, and capturing a socket or an open file throws "Illegal argument in isolate message"

### What to change
1. Move the whole pipeline. Send the raw response String in, decode and map to models inside the isolate, return one compact result.
2. Send bytes as `TransferableTypedData.fromList` — the buffer moves instead of being copied.
3. If the work repeats per keystroke, keep a long-lived worker isolate with a `ReceivePort` instead of respawning.
4. Background isolates have no plugin access until you pass `RootIsolateToken.instance` in and call `BackgroundIsolateBinaryMessenger.ensureInitialized(token)`.

Mental model: an isolate hop is a network call to yourself. Cheap to run, expensive to serialize — so make the message small, not the work.

`WeakReference` and `Expando` let you point at an object without keeping it alive; `Finalizer` only tells you afterwards that one was collected, and it is explicitly allowed never to run.

A plain `Map<String, DecodedImage>` is a strong reference, so nothing in it is ever collected — that is the leak. The weak trio, all in dart:core since Dart 2.17, gives you the alternatives.

### The three tools
- `WeakReference<T>(obj)` — `.target` returns the object, or null once it has been collected. The target cannot be a number, string, bool, record or null: those have no stable identity, so a weak reference to one could never be cleared.
- `Expando<T>` — an identity-keyed side table that does not retain its keys, for attaching data to objects you do not own. Same restrictions on keys.
- `Finalizer<T>(callback)` — `attach(value, token, detach: value)` may call `callback(token)` after `value` becomes unreachable, and `detach(key)` cancels the attachment.

### Why Finalizer is not a destructor
- The SDK's own words: no promises are made that the callback will ever be called. An app that never fills the heap, or simply exits, never runs it.
- The token must not reference the attached object — that keeps it alive forever and the callback can never fire.
- The `Finalizer` itself must stay reachable, so keep it in a static field.
- Callbacks arrive as events, like timers, never mid-expression, and must not throw. For native memory, use `NativeFinalizer` from dart:ffi.

Rule of thumb: correctness lives in explicit lifecycle — `dispose`, `close`, `cancel`. A finalizer is a leak detector or a last-ditch safety net. That is exactly why Flutter makes you write `dispose()` rather than trusting the collector.
